summary.text:
Hinckley & Bosworth's Q1 2026/27 Treasury Management report to Finance & Performance Scrutiny on 24 August is short by the standard we see across Q1s — six pages, no prudential indicators, no liability benchmark, no total CFR, no OLTL, no financing costs ratio — but the loan-book disclosure at §3.11-3.13 is unusually full. The whole 23-loan HRA settlement is tabled with rate, date, principal, interest and reference for every year to 2042; the three §3.12 medium-term loans and the four §3.13 property loans are itemised in the same way.

Because the paper prints so much loan detail, the reconciliation to our file is line-by-line and exact. 26 PWLB loans in our book totalling £82,723,679 at a weighted 3.6747% against the paper's £82,743,679 (§3.2 HRA £52.062m + §3.3 GF £30.681m). Every HRA instalment PW500082-PW500104 matches on rate, date and principal. All three §3.12 medium-term loans match. All four §3.13 property EIPs match. The £13.681m of long-term GF debt not itemised in the tables reconciles against three historical loans in our file (PW504800 £5m 2.96% mat 2063, 507441 £5.381m 2.51% annuity mat 2037, PW493891 £3.3m 4.55% mat 2052). The £20k residual is EIP amortisation on the property loan drawn on 02/02/26 — our balance £980k, the paper's original £1m.

The line worth highlighting to members is what happens in March 2029. The three §3.12 loans mature on 19/02/29, 10/03/29 and 18/03/29 — £18m of bullets in a 30-day window — and a £2.941m HRA instalment matures 28/03/29 on top. Total £20.9m or 25% of the book reprices inside one calendar quarter. The paper's §3.6 rate forecast extends only to September 2027 (5yr PWLB reaching 4.40%), so the market-rate assumption for that refinancing lump isn't in the paper. The §3.13 property borrowing at 5.54-5.86% for 25 years is the other item that a scrutiny question would land on — the April draws priced 27-32bp above the February and March ones.

Balance sheet: only GF CFR is printed (§3.11, £26m forecast for 2026/27), against £30.68m of GF external debt — likely a stock/flow definition question in §3.11 rather than a genuine over-borrowing, but not resolvable from this paper. HRA CFR, total CFR, OLTL and internal borrowing all absent. Not raised in the email — the paper simply isn't the vehicle to close the identity, and the reconciliation elsewhere is strong enough to lead on.

The report author is named (Ilyas Bham, Accountancy Manager x5924) but no email address is published. Report of Head of Finance in the header, no name attached; risk table names 'A Wilson' as owner without a title. Address needs sourcing separately before the email can go.

officer.subject: All 26 of your loans reconcile — and £20.9m reprices in a 30-day window in March 2029
officer.body:
Hi Ilyas,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Q1 2026/27 report to Finance & Performance Scrutiny on 24 August. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paragraph 3.11 tables the whole HRA schedule to 2042 in full, which is unusual and useful.

Every loan reconciles. Your paragraph 3.2 has HRA debt at £52,062,263 and paragraph 3.3 the General Fund at £30,681,416. Our file holds 26 PWLB loans against Hinckley & Bosworth totalling £82,723,679 at a weighted 3.6747%, which ties to £20k on your £82.744m — the residual is EIP amortisation on the property loan drawn on 02/02/26. All sixteen HRA instalments PW500093 through PW500092, the three §3.12 medium-term loans and the four §3.13 property loans all match on rate, date, principal and maturity. Your £13.681m of long-term GF debt not itemised is three loans in our file at 2.51%, 2.96% and 4.55%. It isn't often we can say every line in a book ties — most drift somewhere.

The line worth putting in front of scrutiny is what happens in March 2029. Your three §3.12 loans mature on 19 February 2029, 10 March 2029 and 18 March 2029 — £18m of bullets falling due inside thirty days. Add the £2.941m HRA instalment maturing 28 March 2029 and the total is £20.9m, or 25% of your book, in one calendar quarter. Your §3.6 rate forecast only extends to September 2027 (5-year PWLB reaching 4.40%), so the market-rate assumption for that refinancing point isn't in the paper. Whatever assumption goes in will move the interest-cost projection materially. The dashboard at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard carries the certainty curve at both fixings each morning, so the shape of the current 3-year is a lookup.

The §3.13 property borrowing is the other item that a scrutiny question will land on. Four EIP loans at 5.54%, 5.58%, 5.85% and 5.86%, all 25 years to 2051, funding 18 properties bought so far at £4.058m in total. The two April draws priced 27-32 basis points above the February and March draws — the 25-year curve moved through Q1. Every PWLB loan the sector draws each month is published at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, so where those four sit against contemporaneous 25-year draws by other councils is a lookup rather than research.

Your April-to-June investment return at §3.10 was 3.652% against overnight SONIA 3.730% and 3-month SONIA 3.810% — 8bp under ON on a weighted balance of £2.27m with a 5-day average period. Effectively at market once the liquidity profile is priced. And the interactive liability benchmark pathway at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark takes your figures against the councils we've read that publish theirs — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes.

On the caveats: any break cost we mention is indicative only against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and only the DMO's own quote is binding. We model no MRP or accounting treatment. We hold PWLB only.

On training, three fit this paper: our liability benchmark pathway; Interest rate risk, for the March 2029 refinancing conversation; and Treasury for members, for the scrutiny committee itself. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
